problem_plain: Every computer that handles sensitive work — a cloud server running your bank's code, an AI model processing private medical records, a phone storing your passwords — was designed to run fast, not to keep secrets. Speed-driven design choices, like letting the processor guess what instructions are coming next or sharing a memory bus between multiple users, leave physical fingerprints that an attacker can read without ever breaking any lock. The core problem is that the hardware itself leaks information through time, power draw, and the physical side-effects of its own normal operation. As AI workloads grow and more computation moves to shared cloud chips, the number of places where secrets can leak grows with it.
why_plain: Modern hardware is fast because it reuses resources: the same storage cells, the same memory rows, the same prediction tables, the same memory bus slots get shared between programs, between virtual machines, and between users. That sharing is the physical root of nearly every attack in this section. If two users' data ever passes through the same transistor at overlapping times, the timing or electrical residue of that overlap can carry secret information out to a watching attacker.
approach_plain: Researchers attack the problem from three directions. First, they find and document the new leakage paths that sharing creates — discovering that even ordinary hardware features like a 'fetch data early' engine, a memory prediction table, or an idle power state can bleed secrets across security boundaries. Second, they build defenses that either eliminate the sharing (physically isolating resources by owner) or make the sharing timing-uniform so every user sees identical delays regardless of what the other user is doing. Third, they verify that proposed defenses actually hold up — using automated testing tools, mathematical proofs, and real chip measurements to close the gap between a security claim on paper and security in practice.

groups.heading: Memory row hammering: when reading one cell flips a neighbor
groups.explain: Memory chips store bits as tiny electrical charges in rows of cells. Repeatedly reading (hammering) the same row at high speed disturbs the charge in physically adjacent rows, eventually flipping bits in data that belongs to another program or another virtual machine. The problem has grown worse as chip manufacturing shrinks cells closer together. Many papers here either find new ways to launch this attack despite existing guards, or propose new guards that provably stop the attack without crippling memory performance.

papers.name: HyperHammer
papers.gloss: First attack to hammer memory rows from inside a virtual machine and corrupt the control layer that owns all other virtual machines, bypassing the host's built-in defenses entirely.

papers.name: MOAT
papers.gloss: Tracks how many times each memory row has been read using only 7 bytes of storage per memory bank; two alert thresholds provably stop bit-flip attacks with just 0.28% average slowdown on real server workloads.

papers.name: Chronus
papers.gloss: Moves row-read counters off the main data path so they update in parallel with normal reads, removing the speed penalty that the latest memory standard's built-in counting requirement otherwise causes, while also blocking a known evasion trick called the 'wave attack'.

papers.name: AutoRFM
papers.gloss: Limits protective refreshing to just one slice of memory at a time, letting all other slices keep serving requests normally; cuts slowdown from 33% to 3.1% at the tightest currently accepted safety level.

papers.name: PaCRAM
papers.gloss: Tests 388 real memory chips and shows protective refreshing can run 64% faster than the official specification with only 0.54% more refresh cycles needed, enabling cheaper defenses on existing hardware.

papers.name: QPRAC
papers.gloss: Sorts pending protective-refresh jobs by how many times each row has been hit, so the most-threatened rows are always refreshed first; nearly zero speed impact for normal workloads at the latest memory standard's required safety level.

papers.name: DAPPER
papers.gloss: Randomly shuffles which tracking bucket each memory row maps to, so attackers cannot deliberately inflate another program's counter or trigger spurious protective resets; 0.9% overhead, uses under 100 KB of chip storage per 32 GB of memory.

papers.name: DREAM
papers.gloss: Two strategies to make the most of a grouped-refresh command that the memory standard provides: batch protective work across multiple memory banks to share the stall cost, or group nearby rows so they share one counter, cutting tracker storage by 8 times.

papers.name: MoPAC
papers.gloss: Updates the read counter only on a random fraction of row accesses, then adjusts the safety threshold by the same fraction; cuts the latest memory standard's timing overhead from 10% to under 2% while keeping formal security guarantees intact.

papers.name: TPRAC / PRACLeak
papers.gloss: Shows that the latest memory standard's own built-in row-hammer defense creates a new timing leak — a working key-extraction attack is demonstrated — then fixes it by switching to a fixed-schedule refresh rather than reacting to suspicious access patterns.

papers.name: rhoHammer
papers.gloss: Revives bit-flip attacks on Intel's newest chips where all previous reading-based attacks fail; uses a special 'fetch data early' software instruction to hammer at over 47,000 bit flips per minute where the normal reading approach achieves zero.

papers.name: Citadel
papers.gloss: A software memory allocator that physically places different security domains into non-adjacent memory rows so no hammering attack can reach across; 7.2% memory overhead, zero runtime slowdown, no hardware changes needed.

papers.name: LeakyHammer
papers.gloss: Shows that the protective-refresh pauses used as defenses themselves create measurable timing gaps; builds a hidden data channel running at 39–49 thousand bits per second and a website-fingerprinting attack from those pauses alone.

groups.heading: Speculative execution leaks: the processor guesses wrong and bleeds secrets
groups.explain: To run fast, processors guess the outcome of decision points and start executing instructions ahead of time. If the guess turns out wrong, those instructions are rolled back — but they have already touched shared chip structures, leaving a timing fingerprint. An attacker who controls a neighboring program can read that fingerprint and reconstruct secrets the rolled-back code touched. This class of attack has spawned dozens of variants; the papers here either expose new attack surfaces or build defenses with formal proofs.

papers.name: AMuLeT
papers.gloss: Automatically generates small test programs that probe ahead-of-time execution paths at chip design time, detecting which guess-and-roll-back attack variants a proposed defense fails to block before the chip is manufactured.

Formally proves in a machine-checked proof system that a new compiler transformation protects cryptographic code from all known guess-and-roll-back attack variants, including the return-address prediction attack; overhead under 2% for most cryptographic operations.

papers.name: DejaVuzz
papers.gloss: A chip-level fuzzing tool that swaps physical memory pages at runtime to precisely trigger speculation windows, then uses information-flow tracking to detect when secret data escapes through a timing side channel.

papers.name: SpecASan
papers.gloss: Repurposes ARM's hardware memory-tagging feature — normally used to catch out-of-bounds writes — to pause speculative memory reads that fail a tag check, blocking transient leakage without disabling speculation entirely.

papers.name: Cassandra
papers.gloss: Replaces the guess-ahead predictor entirely for cryptographic code regions by recording and replaying the known, fixed sequence of decisions; eliminates speculative leakage and achieves a net 1.85% average speedup over an unprotected baseline.

papers.name: ShadowBinding
papers.gloss: First working chip-blueprint-level implementation of two leading guess-and-roll-back defenses on a real open-source processor core; finds the combined speed and clock penalty reaches 35% — far higher than prior paper estimates — and proposes a redesigned variant that cuts this to 27%.

Uses compile-time code analysis to pre-approve safe program behaviors, shrinking the set of decisions an AI-based runtime security monitor must watch; makes it practical to distinguish real attacks from false alarms.

groups.heading: Cache and chip-internal side channels: reading secrets through shared timing structures
groups.explain: A cache is a small, fast memory area inside the chip that holds recently used data. Because it is shared between programs, one program's pattern of reading data changes how quickly another program can read its data. Attackers exploit these timing differences — sometimes measuring gaps as small as a few billionths of a second — to reconstruct secret keys, infer which websites a user visited, or track keystrokes. This group includes both classic cache attacks and newer variants that exploit other shared chip structures such as the 'fetch data early' engine, the jump-destination prediction table, and the memory-address prediction unit.

papers.name: Reload+Reload
papers.gloss: Discovers two previously unknown timing leaks inside AMD's encrypted-memory virtual-machine protection: one through cache-flush timing, one through memory-bus contention; combines them to extract full AES-128 encryption keys across virtual machine boundaries.

papers.name: ShadowLoad
papers.gloss: Shows an attacker can write a chosen pattern into the CPU's 'fetch data early' predictor from outside a protected isolated region, causing the victim's predictor to issue unwanted memory fetches that alter the victim's execution timing and reveal information.

papers.name: MDPeek
papers.gloss: Exploits Intel's memory-address prediction unit — a structure that guesses whether a store and a load touch the same address — as a timing side channel against Intel's protected isolated regions, bypassing defenses that try to balance instruction timing.

papers.name: PhasePrint
papers.gloss: Fingerprints individual cloud programmable chips by deliberately inducing tiny timing faults through built-in oscillator circuits and measuring the device-specific fault pattern caused by manufacturing variation; identifies specific chips despite vendor restrictions.

papers.name: FlexProf
papers.gloss: Recovers up to 33% of the throughput lost by fixed-schedule secure memory controllers by splitting time slots into read-optimized and write-optimized types chosen via coarse workload profiling, while preserving timing isolation between virtual machines.

papers.name: SMaCk
papers.gloss: Exploits the processor pipeline flush that occurs when one thread overwrites another thread's cached instructions; timing differences of 150–350 clock cycles enable RSA key recovery in 10 memory traces and full AES key extraction in a single trace.

papers.name: BrokenSleep
papers.gloss: Uses the predictable wake-up delay of processor low-power idle states to carry a hidden data channel and infer keystrokes over a normal network connection — no shared machine or special access required.

Lets an unprivileged attacker force the operating system to pause the victim program at attacker-chosen moments, greatly amplifying the signal quality of timing measurements without any special hardware access.

papers.name: CryptoBTB
papers.gloss: Secures the jump-destination prediction table — a chip structure that remembers where program jumps land — by encrypting its lookup index outside the time-critical prediction path, using a two-level structure to avoid speed loss; 4.3% overhead versus 32% for prior work.

Eliminates timing leakage from the table-lookup step in AI recommendation models by replacing each memory lookup with a tiny neural network calculation; 4 times faster than the standard privacy-preserving memory access technique, with 1000 times less memory overhead.

groups.heading: Trusted execution and confidential computing: verifying what runs inside a protected isolated region
groups.explain: A hardware-isolated region (sometimes called a trusted execution environment) is a walled-off section of the chip where sensitive code can run even if the surrounding operating system is compromised. Cloud providers offer these as 'confidential computing.' The papers here either find gaps in existing walled-region designs or build new mechanisms to close them, including protecting the encrypted data that flows between the processor and memory chips, securing the network path, and making encryption fast enough not to cancel out the security benefit.

papers.name: PipeLLM
papers.gloss: Reduces the encryption overhead of running a large AI model inside a hardware-isolated GPU from up to 88% throughput loss down to under 20%, by predicting which data block the GPU will need next and pre-encrypting it in parallel with ongoing computation.

papers.name: TNIC
papers.gloss: Moves the security trust anchor from the CPU into a smart network card; the card enforces message signing and prevents any sender from broadcasting two contradictory messages, enabling tamper-resistant distributed systems at up to 6 times the throughput of CPU-based protected-region schemes.

papers.name: Pave
papers.gloss: Runs untrusted data-processing code inside a hardware-isolated region with a runtime monitor that tracks every data flow in and out, blocking any flow that would expose user data; users can verify the monitor's integrity remotely using the chip's built-in attestation feature.

papers.name: AIORE
papers.gloss: Cuts encryption overhead on fast-link-to-extra-memory expansion devices used in cloud protected regions by 63% on average, by using fast parallel encryption for frequently accessed pages and standard-compliant encryption only for rarely accessed pages, with re-encryption offloaded to compute inside the memory device itself.

papers.name: SpecMPK
papers.gloss: Allows the instruction that switches memory-region permissions to execute out of order rather than stalling the pipeline, while blocking any speculative access to the newly unlocked region until the permission change is permanent; 12% average speedup for applications with frequent domain switches.

papers.name: Jord
papers.gloss: Runs many small cloud functions inside a single address space using hardware permission-key tags for near-instant isolation, eliminating the millisecond startup delay of separate containers and achieving over 2 times the throughput of current cloud-function systems.

papers.name: NVMePass
papers.gloss: Adds an isolation primitive inside the storage controller so virtual machines can send storage commands directly without going through the host control layer; achieves near-native storage speed for more than 100 virtual machines running simultaneously.

papers.name: Segue & ColorGuard
papers.gloss: Uses two underused x86 hardware features — memory-segment registers for sandbox boundary checks and permission-key tags for coloring separate instances — to cut sandboxing overhead by 45% and fit 15 times more concurrent sandboxes per address space.

groups.heading: Hardware verification and formal security proofs: catching bugs before the chip ships
groups.explain: A security flaw in a chip design cannot be patched with a software update — it lives in billions of devices until they are replaced. This group of papers builds tools and methods to prove that a proposed hardware design is secure before manufacturing begins. Some use automatic test-program generation to probe for weaknesses; others use mathematical solvers or theorem provers to verify correctness; one automatically generates correct operating-system code from a formal chip description.

papers.name: Velosiraptor
papers.gloss: Automatically generates the operating system code that configures hardware memory-protection units directly from a formal chip specification, eliminating the error-prone manual translation step that has historically introduced security bugs.

papers.name: SylQ-SV
papers.gloss: Speeds up the process of mathematically exploring all possible states of a hardware chip design by caching and reusing solver answers across similar paths; achieves up to 17% runtime reduction while covering the full chip-description language including security assertions.

papers.name: CapChecker / Adaptive CHERI
papers.gloss: An adapter placed on the connection between an accelerator chip and system memory that enforces strict memory-bounds checking — ensuring every pointer stays within its allowed region — on any accelerator without modifying the accelerator itself; 1.4% average overhead.

papers.name: Let-Me-In (LMI)
papers.gloss: Encodes each allocation's size and starting address directly into the unused high bits of GPU memory pointers, enabling hardware bounds checks on every GPU memory access with negligible overhead across thousands of parallel threads.

papers.name: Palermo
papers.gloss: Redesigns the privacy-preserving memory access protocol — a method that hides which memory addresses a program reads by shuffling requests — to allow overlapping requests instead of waiting for each to finish; achieves 2.9 times the speed of the sequential baseline with a hardware controller occupying under 2% of chip area.

groups.heading: Fuzzing and automated bug-finding: probing systems faster than humans can
groups.explain: Security researchers find bugs by sending millions of unexpected inputs to a system and watching for crashes or misbehavior — a process called fuzzing. The challenge is that interesting bugs often hide behind specific combinations of inputs, so naive random testing misses them. The papers here use machine learning and statistical methods to guide the fuzzer toward unexplored corners of a program, and one applies probability theory to find concurrency bugs that only appear when program threads happen to interleave in rare orders.

papers.name: Snowplow
papers.gloss: Trains a machine learning model on operating-system source code to predict which test-input mutations are most likely to reach untested code paths, improving vulnerability discovery rate over handcoded guessing rules.

papers.name: KernelGPT
papers.gloss: Uses a large language model to automatically write and iteratively repair the structured descriptions of operating-system entry points that a fuzzer needs as input, dramatically expanding which parts of the operating system can be tested.

papers.name: SURW
papers.gloss: A concurrency-testing method with a provable guarantee of uniform sampling across all possible thread orderings, finding rare data-race bugs that biased random methods miss on standard concurrency test suites.

groups.heading: Supply-chain and software-level AI security: attacks that arrive before the model runs
groups.explain: Not all attacks target hardware. A machine learning model is assembled from dozens of open-source libraries, pre-trained weights downloaded from the internet, and automated pipelines. If any upstream piece is compromised, the model can be silently altered to behave differently for specific inputs — a backdoor — or made to leak its own internal weights through its outputs. These papers document the scale of that risk in today's AI ecosystem and explore ways to compute on private data without ever exposing it.

papers.gloss: Shows a malicious Python package can silently rewrite deep learning library internals at import time to inject backdoors or steal model weights; a survey of 549,000 public code issues finds the machine learning community is no more security-aware than the general software community, despite a larger chain of untrusted dependencies.

papers.name: Orion
papers.gloss: An automated tool that translates a standard PyTorch model into a form of encrypted computation — where all math runs on scrambled numbers so the server never sees the real inputs or outputs — and is the first to compile an object-detection model with 139 million parameters, running 2.4 times faster than prior tools.

papers.name: DPUaudit
papers.gloss: Moves system audit log collection off the monitored machine and into a physically separate smart network card that pulls log data over the wire connection between chips, reducing monitoring overhead from over 10% down to an average of 2.1%.

Applies statistical hypothesis testing with provable accuracy bounds to decide exactly when a classification model can safely stop processing early, avoiding wasted computation while guaranteeing the accuracy loss stays within a proven statistical limit.

connect: Every attack in this section ultimately exploits the same physical fact that also bottlenecks AI performance: data must move through shared wires, shared fast on-chip memory areas, and shared memory rows, and every time two users share the same wire, the timing of that sharing carries a signal. The same memory-bus contention that limits how fast a chip can feed a large AI model is the contention that lets a spying program read timing differences measured in billionths of a second — security and performance are two faces of the same data-movement problem.
